system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2179-08-16 21:54:00 to 2179-08-18 16:24:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old female with a history of end-stage renal disease, diastolic heart failure, and diabetes was admitted for acute shortness of breath that woke her from sleep. She presented with hypertensive urgency, tachycardia, and clinical signs of fluid overload. A chest X-ray confirmed pulmonary edema, and she was treated with BiPAP, intravenous diuretics, and nitroglycerin. She underwent hemodialysis, which removed 3.2 liters of fluid, leading to rapid improvement in respiratory status and hemodynamic stability. Her medications were adjusted, including discontinuation of midodrine, initiation of extended-release metoprolol, and addition of aspirin. She was discharged home with nursing services after education on daily weight monitoring, fluid and sodium restriction, and adherence to dialysis.
problems: Acute on chronic diastolic heart failure
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage V or end stage renal disease
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

Stable, afebrile.
 
Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted for shortness of breath. This improved greatly 
with hemodialysis. You have a very difficult balance of fluids 
to maintain. It is important to adhere to your sodium (salt) and 
fluid restriction in order to prevent fluid from building up in 
your body. Please be careful to take all of your medications and 
maintain your dialysis schedule.

You have an additional two days of CEFPODOXIME to take for 
treating your urinary tract infection. Please take this 
medication after your dialysis on ___.

You are being given an additional medication called Imdur. You 
should take this medication (30mg by mouth) on ___ morning. 
This medication is to help prevent hig blood pressure and fluid 
build-up on ___, prior to your hemodialysis on ___. Your 
other medications were not changed. Please resume taking them as 
before.

Please adhere to your follow-up appointments. They are important 
for managing your long-term health.

Please return to the hospital or call your doctor if you have 
temperature greater than 101, shortness of breath, worsening 
difficulty with swallowing, chest pain, abdominal pain, 
diarrhea, or any other symptoms that you are concerned about.
 
Followup Instructions:

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I was watching a football game when I suddenly couldn’t catch my breath. I couldn’t even finish a sentence. EMS came and said my blood pressure was really high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your blood pressure was 220 when EMS arrived. They gave you nitroglycerin and put you on CPAP to help you breathe. By the time you got here, your pressure had come down, and your oxygen levels were improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. I felt a little better once they gave me that mask. But I was so scared. Is this another fluid overload episode?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like flash pulmonary edema, likely due to high blood pressure and your heart’s difficulty relaxing—your diastolic heart failure. Your lungs are holding extra fluid, which is why you felt so short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this before, especially before dialysis on Mondays. I didn’t miss my meds this morning—my nurse helps me with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. We checked your labs, and your kidney function is consistent with your usual ESRD. Creatinine was 6.8, which is expected. We’ve scheduled you for hemodialysis tomorrow morning to remove the extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I usually feel much better after dialysis. But why does this keep happening on Mondays?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because you go two days between dialysis—Saturday to Monday—fluid builds up faster. We’re going to add a new medication called Imdur, a long-acting nitrate, to take on Sundays to help prevent this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Will that help with my blood pressure too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it helps lower the pressure in your heart and blood vessels, reducing fluid buildup. We’re keeping you on your usual meds: valsartan, lisinopril, and metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been on those for years. What about my warfarin and insulin? Should I take them tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll get your usual doses. We’re monitoring your INR closely. Your blood sugar was 168 earlier—within range—so your insulin dose stays the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been trying to manage everything, but it’s a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You’re doing well with your care team. We’ll keep you on CPAP tonight to support your breathing and monitor your oxygen levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m okay, but I felt short of breath again a little while ago, even though my oxygen was good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. Your oxygen was 100%, but you felt dyspneic. We put you on BiPAP temporarily and gave a bit of nitropaste because your blood pressure was up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It helped. I felt better once I got the BiPAP. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, sometimes patients feel breathless even with good oxygen levels, especially with heart strain. Now that you’re calm and your pressure is down, we’re weaning off support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will I have dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s scheduled for 8 AM. Once you start, you should feel much better. We expect good fluid removal, like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your dialysis went well. You’re off BiPAP now and back on your usual 3 liters of oxygen. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I can breathe easily now. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray this morning showed some improvement in the fluid, though there are still mild signs of edema and small pleural effusions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that normal after dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it takes time for all the fluid to clear. The X-ray also showed some nodular spots in your lungs—could be infection, but we’re not sure yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Infection? I don’t have a fever or cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, and your white count is only slightly elevated. But we found Klebsiella in a urine culture from your last admission. You already got one dose of ceftriaxone in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I have a UTI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely. Even though you don’t have symptoms, we’re treating it with a short course of cefpodoxime—two days, starting after your next dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll take it as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning look good. Creatinine dropped to 5.2, and your electrolytes are stable. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning. You’ll go home with nursing services to help with meds and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I live alone, so that helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re stable and afebrile. We’re ready to discharge you. Remember to take your new Imdur every Sunday morning to help prevent Monday crises.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 30 mg on Sunday. And cefpodoxime after dialysis for two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Keep up with fluid and salt limits, daily weights, and your dialysis schedule. Call us if you have fever, chest pain, or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor. I’ll try to make it through the long gap better next time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing a great job managing a tough condition. We’re here to help. Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old female with a history of end-stage renal disease, diastolic heart failure, and diabetes was admitted for acute shortness of breath that began suddenly while watching television. She presented with hypertensive urgency and signs of pulmonary edema. EMS initiated CPAP and nitroglycerin, which improved her symptoms. In the hospital, she was managed with oxygen support, antihypertensives, and scheduled hemodialysis, which led to significant improvement in her respiratory status and fluid balance. A urine culture from a prior admission grew Klebsiella, prompting a short course of oral antibiotics. She was discharged home with nursing services, new instructions for a Sunday dose of Imdur to prevent interdialytic fluid overload, and education on medication adherence, fluid restriction, and infection monitoring.
